facts.statement: Use high beams when no vehicle is oncoming, while observing the separate low-beam guidance for following and heavy traffic.

evidence.excerpt: Use your high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles.
Use your low beams within 200 feet when following another vehicle or when in heavy traffic.

facts.statement: The handbook says high beams provide twice the viewing distance of low beams.

evidence.excerpt:
High beams let you see twice as 
far as low beams.

facts.statement: High-beam visibility is especially useful on unfamiliar roads, in work zones and where people may be beside the road.

evidence.excerpt:
It is important to use high beams on unfamiliar roads, in construction areas or 
where there may be people along the side of the road.

facts.statement: Dim high beams when an approaching vehicle is about one block away.

evidence.excerpt:
Dim your high beams whenever you come within about a one-block distance of an oncoming 
vehicle.

facts.statement: When following within 200 feet, or driving in heavy traffic, switch to low beams.

evidence.excerpt: Use your low beams within 200 feet when following another vehicle or when in heavy traffic.

facts.statement: Choose low beams in fog, heavy snowfall or heavy rain because high-beam reflections create glare.

evidence.excerpt:
Use the low beams in fog or when it is snowing or raining hard.  Light from high beams will 
reflect back, causing glare and making it more difficult to see ahead.

facts.statement: Use the vehicle’s fog lights too, if it has them, in the described fog, heavy snow or heavy rain.

evidence.excerpt:
Some vehicles have fog 
lights that you also should use under these conditions.

facts.statement: Parking lamps alone are unsuitable for driving; they serve parked vehicles.

evidence.excerpt: Do not drive at any time with only your parking lights on.  Parking lights are for parking only.

facts.statement: Turn on headlights when other road users are difficult to see, helping them see your vehicle too.

evidence.excerpt:
Remember to turn on your headlights 
whenever you have trouble seeing others.  If you have trouble seeing them, they may be having trouble 
seeing you.

facts.statement: When you use windshield wipers, also switch on the headlights.

evidence.excerpt:
Remember, if you turn on your wipers, 
turn on your headlights.

facts.statement: Switch on headlights as daylight starts fading so other drivers can see you.

evidence.excerpt:
Turn on your headlights when it begins to get dark.  Even if you turn them on a little early, you 
will help other drivers see you.

facts.statement: Use headlights while traveling away from sunrise or sunset because drivers facing you may struggle to see you.

evidence.excerpt:
When driving away from a rising or setting sun, turn on your headlights.  Drivers coming towards 
you may have trouble seeing your vehicle.

facts.statement: A brief headlight flick, when needed, can alert another road user to your presence.

evidence.excerpt:
If needed, 
flick your headlights to alert other road users you are there.

facts.statement: Use the horn when doing so can prevent a collision; without immediate danger, use a light tap.

evidence.excerpt:
Use it whenever it will help prevent an accident.  If there is no immediate danger, a light tap on 
the horn should be all you need.

facts.statement: A light horn tap can alert a pedestrian or cyclist who appears headed into your travel lane.

evidence.excerpt: when a person on foot or on a bike appears to be moving into your lane of travel

facts.statement: When overtaking a driver who begins moving into your lane, a light horn tap can warn that driver.

evidence.excerpt: when you are passing a driver who starts to turn into your lane

facts.statement: A light horn tap can help when a driver is inattentive or may not see your vehicle.

evidence.excerpt: when a driver is not paying attention or may have trouble seeing you

facts.statement: The handbook suggests a light horn tap near a blind hill, sharp bend or narrow-alley exit where you cannot see ahead.

evidence.excerpt:
when coming to a place where you cannot see what is ahead — like a steep hill, a sharp curve or 
exiting a narrow alley

facts.statement: In danger, use a sharp horn blast if a child or older person is about to enter the street.

evidence.excerpt: when a child or older person is about to walk, run or ride into the street
If there is danger, do not be afraid to sound a SHARP BLAST on your horn.  Do this:

facts.statement: In danger, use a sharp horn blast when another vehicle may hit you.

evidence.excerpt: when another vehicle is in danger of hitting you
If there is danger, do not be afraid to sound a SHARP BLAST on your horn.  Do this:

facts.statement: In danger, use a sharp horn blast if your uncontrolled vehicle is heading toward someone.

evidence.excerpt: when you have lost control of your vehicle and are moving towards someone
If there is danger, do not be afraid to sound a SHARP BLAST on your horn.  Do this:

facts.statement: Use a turn signal before a lane change, either turn, a merge or parking.

evidence.excerpt:
You 
should use your turn signals before you change lanes, turn right or left, merge into traffic or park.

facts.statement: Signal each change of direction even when no other road user is visible.

evidence.excerpt:
Signal even when you do not see 
anyone else around.  It is easy to miss someone who needs to know what you are doing.

facts.statement: Begin the turn signal no less than 100 feet before turning.

evidence.excerpt: Signal at least 100 feet before you make your turn.

facts.statement: If a vehicle may enter between you and the intended turn, wait until you pass it before signaling to avoid implying an earlier turn.

evidence.excerpt:
If another vehicle is about to enter the street between you and where you plan to turn, wait until 
you have passed it to signal your turn.

facts.statement: After turning or changing lanes, check that the signal has canceled and switch it off yourself if necessary.

evidence.excerpt:
After you have made a turn or lane change, make sure your turn signal is off.  After small turns, 
the signals may not turn off by themselves.

facts.statement: Brake lamps tell following drivers that your vehicle is slowing.

evidence.excerpt: Your brake lights let people know that you are slowing down.

facts.statement: Begin slowing as early as safety permits; if time allows, warn the following driver before a sudden slowdown or stop.

evidence.excerpt:
Always 
slow down as early as it is safe to do so.  Do not slow down or stop suddenly without signaling to the 
driver behind you (if you have time).

facts.statement: For a highway breakdown, make the stopped vehicle visible to other drivers.

evidence.excerpt:
If your vehicle breaks down on a highway, make sure that other drivers can see 
it.

facts.statement: If available, use a phone or two-way radio to tell authorities about your own or another vehicle’s breakdown.

evidence.excerpt:
If available, use your 2-way radio or telephone to notify authorities that your vehicle or someone else has 
broken down.

facts.statement: Roadside emergency signs may provide a telephone number or CB channel for assistance.

evidence.excerpt:
Many roadways have signs that tell you the CB channel or telephone number to call in an 
emergency.

facts.statement: When vehicle trouble forces a stop, leave the road and move away from traffic if possible.

evidence.excerpt: Get your vehicle off the road and away from traffic if at all possible

facts.statement: Activate emergency flashers to indicate vehicle trouble.

evidence.excerpt: Turn on your emergency flashers to show you are having trouble

facts.statement: If unable to leave the roadway, try to stop where others can see the vehicle, avoiding the far side of a hill or bend.

evidence.excerpt:
Try to stop where other drivers have a clear view of your vehicle if you cannot get your vehicle off 
the roadway.  (Do not stop just over a hill or just around a curve.)

facts.statement: The manual advises putting warning flares behind a disabled vehicle to give others time to change lanes.

evidence.excerpt:
Try to warn other road users that your vehicle is there.  Place emergency flares behind the vehicle.  
This allows other drivers to change lanes if necessary.

facts.statement: Stay out of the roadway and do not change a tire from inside a traffic lane.

evidence.excerpt: Never stand in the roadway.  Do not try to change a tire if it means you have to be in a traffic lane.

facts.statement: Avoid traveling beside and slightly behind another vehicle, where its driver may not see you.

evidence.excerpt:
Try to avoid driving on either side and slightly to the rear of another vehicle.  You will be in 
his/her blind spot.

facts.statement: Adjust forward or backward relative to another vehicle so its driver can see you more easily.

evidence.excerpt:
Either speed up or drop back so the other driver can see your vehicle more 
easily.

facts.statement: While passing, minimize the time spent in the other driver’s blind spot.

evidence.excerpt: When passing another vehicle, get through the other driver’s blind spot as quickly as you can.

facts.statement: Avoid remaining alongside a bus or large truck because its driver has substantial blind areas.

evidence.excerpt: Never stay along side a large vehicle such as a truck or bus.  These vehicles have large blind spots

facts.statement: Warn other drivers before changing direction or slowing so they have time to respond.

evidence.excerpt:
You must warn them when you are 
going to change direction or slow down.  This will give them time to react if needed

facts.statement: A turn signal left on after the maneuver can falsely suggest another planned turn.

evidence.excerpt:
If you 
don’t, others might think you plan to turn again.

facts.statement: Higher speed increases the distance needed to turn, slow down or stop.

evidence.excerpt: The faster your vehicle is going, the more distance it will take to turn, slow or stop.

facts.statement: Reduce speed before a sharp bend and when the surface is slippery or holds standing water.

evidence.excerpt:
you must slow down before a 
sharp curve, when the roadway is slippery and when there is standing water on the road.

facts.statement: Tire grip depends on both tire type and condition and road-surface type and condition.

evidence.excerpt:
How good a grip the tires have with 
the road depends on the type and condition of the tires and the type and condition of the road surface.

facts.statement: Keep tires sound and properly inflated; consult the vehicle’s manual for the correct pressure.

evidence.excerpt:
It is important that the tires be in good condition and have enough air in them. See the vehicle owner’s 
manual for correct tire pressure.

facts.statement: On dirt or gravel, reduce speed because grip is poorer, stopping takes longer and turning skids are easier than on asphalt or concrete.

evidence.excerpt:
You do not have as much traction on gravel or dirt roads as you do on concrete or asphalt roads.  When 
driving on gravel or dirt, you must slow down.  It will take you much longer to stop and it is much easier 
to skid when turning.

facts.statement: Slow before entering a curve; braking while curving can cause a skid.

evidence.excerpt:
Always slow down before you enter the curve so you do not have to brake in the curve.  Braking in a 
curve can cause the vehicle to skid.

facts.statement: Reduce speed when rain, snow or sleet first begins because tire grip decreases.

evidence.excerpt: Slow down at the first sign of rain, snow or sleet.  These all make the roadway slippery.

facts.statement: The handbook recommends lowering speed by about 10 mph on wet pavement.

evidence.excerpt: On a wet road you should reduce your speed about 10 mph.

facts.statement: For packed snow, the handbook recommends reducing speed to half.

evidence.excerpt:
On packed snow you should 
cut your speed in half.

facts.statement: The handbook recommends snow tires or chains when snow covers the road.

evidence.excerpt: Use snow tires or chains when the road has snow on it.

facts.statement: On ice, the handbook advises crawling slowly and avoiding the trip if possible.

evidence.excerpt:
On ice, you must slow to a 
crawl.  It is very dangerous to drive on ice. 
If at all possible, do not drive when the roads are icy.

facts.statement: Studded-tire permission varies by area and road because the studs can damage pavement.

evidence.excerpt:
In some areas where there is a lot of icy weather, 
special studded tires are allowed.  Because these tires can cause road damage, they are not allowed in 
many areas or on certain roads.

facts.statement: Cold, wet shaded areas can freeze before other places and remain icy longer.

evidence.excerpt: On cold, wet days shady spots can be icy.  These areas freeze first and dry out last.

facts.statement: Bridge and overpass pavement can be icy while surrounding roads are clear because it lacks insulating earth underneath.

evidence.excerpt:
The pavement on bridges can be icy 
even when other pavement is not.  This is because bridges do not have earth underneath them to 
help insulate them against the cold

facts.statement: Near freezing, wet ice can be more slippery than ice at much colder temperatures.

evidence.excerpt:
When the temperature is around the freezing point, ice can become wet. This makes it more 
slippery than at temperatures well below freezing.

facts.statement: At the start of hot-weather rain, surfaced oil can make pavement especially slick until rain washes it away.

evidence.excerpt:
If it starts to rain on a hot day, pavement can be very slippery for the first few minutes. Heat 
causes the oil in the asphalt to come to the surface.

facts.statement: The manual says most tires retain good wet-road grip to about 35 mph; rising speed can make tires ride on water, called hydroplaning.

evidence.excerpt:
most tires have good traction up to about 35 
mph.  However as you go faster, your tires will start to ride up on the water, like water skis.  This is called 
“hydroplaning.”

facts.statement: In heavy rain, the handbook says tires may lose all road grip at roughly 50 mph.

evidence.excerpt: In a heavy rain, your tires can lose all traction with the road at about 50 mph.

facts.statement: Bald or heavily worn tires can lose grip at considerably lower speeds than the preceding wet-road examples.

evidence.excerpt: badly worn tires will lose traction at much lower speeds.
Bald or

facts.statement: To reduce hydroplaning risk, slow down during rain or on a wet road.

evidence.excerpt:
The best way to keep from hydroplaning is to 
slow down in the rain or when the road is wet.

facts.statement: If tires seem to lose road grip, gradually release the accelerator.

evidence.excerpt: If it feels like your tires have lost traction with the surface of the road you should:
Ease your foot off the gas pedal.

facts.statement: After traction loss, hold the wheel straight; turn only for an emergency and then do so slowly.

evidence.excerpt:
Keep the steering wheel straight.  Only try to turn if it’s an emergency.  If you must turn, do it 
slowly

facts.statement: After traction loss, avoid trying to brake or turn until grip returns, subject to the stated emergency-turn qualification.

evidence.excerpt: Do not try to stop or turn until your tires are gripping the road again.
Only try to turn if it’s an emergency.

facts.statement: With good tires, good brakes and dry pavement, reacting and stopping at 50 mph can require about 400 feet.

evidence.excerpt:
If you have good tires and brakes and dry 
pavement:

At 50 mph, it can take about 400 feet to react to something you see and bring your vehicle to a 
stop.

facts.statement: With good tires, good brakes and dry pavement, stopping from 30 mph can require about 200 feet.

evidence.excerpt:
If you have good tires and brakes and dry 
pavement:
At 30 mph, it can take about 200 feet to stop.

facts.statement: Seeing less than 400 feet ahead may make 50 mph unsafe; seeing less than 200 feet ahead may make 30 mph unsafe.

evidence.excerpt:
If you cannot see 400 feet ahead, it means you may not be driving safely at 50 mph.  If you cannot see 
200 feet ahead, you may not be driving safely at 30 mph.

facts.statement: At night, travel slowly enough to stop inside the area illuminated by your headlights.

evidence.excerpt: You must be able to stop within the distance you can see ahead with your headlights.

facts.statement: The manual estimates about 400 feet of headlight visibility and gives about 50 mph as its stopping-within-that-distance example.

evidence.excerpt:
headlights will let you see about 400 feet ahead.  You should drive at a speed that allows you to stop 
within this distance or about 50 mph.

facts.statement: In very heavy rain, a snowstorm or dense fog, visibility may be only about 200 feet; the handbook says not to exceed 30 mph when unable to see farther.

evidence.excerpt:
In a very heavy rain, snowstorm or thick fog, you may not be able to see much more 
than 200 feet ahead.  When you cannot see any farther than that, you cannot safely drive faster than 30 
mph.

facts.statement: If a downpour prevents adequate visibility for driving, leave the road at a safe place and wait for improvement.

evidence.excerpt:
In a very heavy downpour, you may not be able to see well enough to drive. If this happens, pull off 
the road in a safe place and wait until it clears.

facts.statement: Approach a hillcrest or blind curve at a speed that lets you stop for an unseen obstruction.

evidence.excerpt:
Whenever you come to a hill or curve where you cannot see over or around, 
adjust your speed so you can stop if necessary.

facts.statement: Allow as much room as possible beside parked vehicles because people may step out or emerge between them.

evidence.excerpt:
People may be ready 
to get out of a vehicle or walk out from between parked vehicles. Give parked vehicles as much room as 
you can.

facts.statement: For the four-second sight-distance check, choose the farthest stationary object you can see clearly and count four seconds toward it.

evidence.excerpt:
Pick out a stationary object as far ahead 
as you can clearly see

Start counting “one-one-thousand, 
two-one-thousand, three-one-thousand, four-one-thousand.”

facts.statement: If you reach that sight-distance marker before finishing four seconds, reduce speed.

evidence.excerpt:
If you reach the object before you finish 
saying “four-one-thousand,” you need to slow down.

facts.statement: Use the four-second sight-distance check at night to avoid driving beyond useful headlight visibility.

evidence.excerpt: You should also use the “Four Second Sight Distance Rule” at night

facts.statement: Watch roadway edges and animal-crossing signs for wildlife; slow down after seeing struck animals because the area may be a crossing.

evidence.excerpt:
Watch the edges of the highway for wildlife that are about to cross. Watch for 
animal crossing signs.

And if you 
see animals that have been hit, slow down. You may be in an animal crossing area.

facts.statement: The manual lists deer, elk, pronghorn antelope, black bears and cougars among large-animal road hazards in New Mexico.

evidence.excerpt:
Watch out for these large game animals: 
deer, elk, pronghorn antelope, black bears, and cougars.

facts.statement: The source places large game, especially deer, statewide; elk mainly in the western three-quarters, antelope in eastern/open plains and bears or cougars in mountains.

evidence.excerpt:
Large game animals (especially deer) live all over the state. Watch for elk in the western three-quarters of 
the state. Watch for antelope in the eastern part of the state or in open plains. And keep an eye out for 
black bears and cougars in the mountains.

facts.statement: Be especially alert for wildlife around dawn, dusk and the early hours of darkness.

evidence.excerpt: Be especially watchful for wildlife at dawn, dusk, and in the first few hours after darkness falls.

facts.statement: Do not assume an animal will move away; after one animal crosses, expect others.

evidence.excerpt: Assume that animals won’t get out of your way.
Remember that where one animal is crossing, there may be more.

facts.statement: Hoofed animals may slow on slick surfaces, so prepare to slow and let them cross.

evidence.excerpt:
Animals with hooves, such as deer, often slow down on slick surfaces. So be ready to slow down 
to let them cross.

facts.statement: Traveling faster than surrounding traffic creates repeated passing exposure; reduce speed to keep pace.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are going faster than traffic, you will have to keep passing others.  Each 
time you pass someone, there is a chance for a collision.

Slow down and keep pace 
with other traffic.

facts.statement: Driving far slower than surrounding traffic can cause bunching and passing; if a queue forms behind you, pull over when safe to let it pass.

evidence.excerpt:
If vehicles are piled-up behind you, pull over when 
safe to do so and let them pass.
Going much slower than other vehicles can be just as bad as speeding.

facts.statement: When merging, try to match traffic speed and use the entry ramp to accelerate before joining the roadway.

evidence.excerpt: When you merge with traffic, try to enter at the same speed that traffic is moving.

Use the ramp to 
reach the speed of other vehicles before you pull onto the road.

facts.statement: Avoid reaching the ramp’s end and stopping because you lose acceleration room and may surprise drivers behind.

evidence.excerpt:
Do not drive to the end of the ramp and 
stop or you will not have enough room to get up to the speed of traffic.  Also, drivers behind you will not 
expect you to stop.

facts.statement: If waiting for a merge gap is necessary, slow on the ramp while preserving room to accelerate before joining.

evidence.excerpt:
have to wait for space to enter a roadway, slow down on the ramp so you have some room to speed-up 
before you have to merge.
If you

facts.statement: Maintain traffic speed on the main roadway and move onto the exit ramp before reducing speed.

evidence.excerpt:
Keep up with the speed of traffic as long as you are on the main road.  If the road you 
are traveling has exit ramps, do not slow down until you move onto the exit ramp.

facts.statement: For a turn from a fast two-lane road with following traffic, avoid slowing too early; tap the brakes and reduce speed promptly but safely.

evidence.excerpt:
When you turn from a 
high speed, two-lane roadway, try not to slow down too early if you have traffic following you.  Tap your 
brakes and reduce your speed quickly but safely.

facts.statement: Spot slow vehicles early enough to change lanes or reduce speed without a sudden slowdown.

evidence.excerpt:
If you spot these vehicles early, you have time to change lanes or slow down safely.  Slowing 
suddenly can cause a traffic accident.

facts.statement: Large trucks and small low-powered cars may lose speed on steep grades and need longer to accelerate into traffic.

evidence.excerpt:
Watch for large trucks and small underpowered cars on steep grades or when they are entering 
traffic.  They can lose speed on long or steep hills

facts.statement: The handbook describes tractors, animal-drawn vehicles and road-maintenance vehicles as usually traveling 25 mph or less and displaying an orange triangular slow-vehicle decal.

evidence.excerpt:
Farm tractors, animal-drawn vehicles and roadway maintenance vehicles usually go 25 mph or 
less.  These vehicles should have a slow-moving vehicle decal (an orange triangle) on the back.

facts.statement: Where traffic or people crowd the available maneuvering space, reduce speed to allow response time.

evidence.excerpt:
Wherever people or traffic gather, your room to maneuver is limited.  You need to lower 
your speed to have time to react in a crowded space.

facts.statement: Busy shopping areas, parking lots, downtown streets and rush-hour traffic can require a slower speed.

evidence.excerpt: Shopping centers, parking lots and downtown areas—These are busy areas
Rush Hours—Rush hours often have heavy traffic

facts.statement: Narrow bridges and tunnels bring opposing vehicles closer together and may require slowing.

evidence.excerpt: Narrow bridges and tunnels—Vehicles approaching each other are closer together.

facts.statement: At toll plazas, anticipate lane changes, stops, acceleration and changing lane counts.

evidence.excerpt:
Toll plazas—Vehicles are changing lanes and preparing to stop and then speeding-up again when 
leaving the plaza. The number of lanes could change both before and after the plaza.

facts.statement: Near schools, playgrounds and homes, watch for children entering the street without looking.

evidence.excerpt:
Schools, playgrounds and residential streets—These areas often have children present. Always be 
alert for children crossing the street or running or riding into the street without looking.

facts.statement: At railroad crossings, verify no train is coming and enough space exists to clear the crossing; slow for a rough crossing surface.

evidence.excerpt:
Railroad crossings—you need to make sure that there are no trains coming and that you have room 
to cross.  Some crossings are bumpy so you need to slow down to safely cross.
